The verb rendered "withhold" (yikhleh) follows III-He spelling and inflection while carrying the sense of the III-Aleph root kala' ("withhold, restrain").
notes.23:11: The three occurrences of the Qal perfect of natan ("I give") function as performative perfects, effecting a formal offer or legal declaration in the act of speaking (likewise in 23:13).
notes.23:13: The Hebrew opening (literally "only if you, would that, listen to me") combines an elliptical conditional ("if you [will]") with the optative particle lu uniquely placed before the imperative "listen to me" to express urgent politeness.
notes.23:16: The commercial idiom "current with the merchant" (literally "passing to the merchant," with singular collective soher) refers to weighed silver of standard purity and value accepted in trade.
notes.23:17: The Qal verb wayyaqom ("stood confirmed," literally "arose/stood," repeated in 23:20) is a legal term for property becoming validly transferred and permanently established in a buyer's ownership.
notes.24:12: The Hiphil imperative of qarah ("bring about success") literally means "cause to happen" or "arrange a favorable encounter."
notes.24:21: The participle translated "watching ... in wonder" is a rare Hithpael form of sha'ah (with metathesis of the prefix t and initial shin), conveying intent, silent amazement.
notes.24:22: Hebrew beka denotes a half-shekel weight; in the second clause, "ten of gold" idiomatically leaves the unit "shekels" unstated.
notes.24:32: The unexpressed third-person singular subject of "unharnessed" and "gave" shifts implicitly from the servant back to his host, Laban.
notes.24:33: Ketiv/Qere: the written text preserves an unusual passive spelling of sim ("set"), while the read text (qere, translated here) gives the regular Hophal passive wayyiqtol "was set."
notes.24:43: Hebrew almah denotes a marriageable unmarried young woman, distinct from na'arah ("young woman") used in verses 14, 16, 28, 55, and 57.
notes.24:48: Hebrew "daughter of my master's brother" uses kinship terms broadly, since Rebekah is the granddaughter of Abraham's brother Nahor.
notes.24:62: Hebrew mibbo' ("from the approach to" or "from coming to") follows the Masoretic Text; Beer-lahai-roi is the well named in Genesis 16:14.
notes.24:63: The verb translated "meditate" (Hebrew lasuach) occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible; its exact sense is uncertain, with proposals including "meditate" (linked to siach) and "stroll" or "walk about."
notes.24:67: Hebrew literally reads "into the tent, Sarah his mother" (a rare appositional construct) and concludes with "after his mother," with her death implied from context.
notes.25:8: Hebrew literally reads "old and satisfied" (or "full"), without the phrase "of days" or "of years" supplied by some ancient versions.
notes.25:18: The verb rendered "he settled" is literally "he fell" (Qal perfect of naphal), used idiomatically of encamping or having one's territorial lot fall; "opposite" (literally "upon the face of") can also carry the nuance "east of" or "in defiance of."
notes.25:21: The verbs "pleaded" and "granted his plea" pair the Qal and Niphal stems of the same root ('atar), the Niphal carrying a tolerative sense ("let Himself be pleaded with").
notes.25:23: The ketiv (written form) reads gyym, likely an unusual spelling variant, while the qere (read form) is goyim ("nations"), which is translated here.
notes.25:30: The verb "let me gulp down" (Hiphil imperative of la'at) occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and suggests greedy swallowing; the name Edom ("red") plays on Esau's repeated word 'adom ("red").
notes.26:4: The verb "will bless themselves" is in the Hithpael stem (of barak), which is primarily reflexive—invoking your offspring's name in blessing—though it can also bear a passive sense ("will be blessed").
notes.26:8: The participle "caressing" (Piel of tsahaq, "laugh, play intimately") plays on the name Isaac (Yitshaq, from the same root).
notes.26:12: Hebrew me'ah she'arim literally means "a hundred measures" (or "portions"), an idiom for a hundredfold return on the seed sown.
notes.26:20: The well names in vv. 20-22 reflect Isaac's experiences: Esek means "Contention" (playing on the Hithpael verb "contended"), Sitnah means "Opposition" or "Hostility," and Rehoboth means "Broad Places" (playing on the Hiphil verb "has made room").
notes.26:29: The clause "that you will do us no harm" literally begins "if you do harm to us," the standard Hebrew oath formula that implies a curse if the stipulation is broken.
notes.27:3: Ketiv reads a feminine form or "provisions," while qere reads the standard masculine noun "game," matching the rest of the chapter. The noun rendered "quiver" occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and derives from a root meaning "to hang."
notes.27:29: Ketiv writes a singular (or defective plural) verb for "bow down," while qere reads the explicit plural matching the plural subject "nations."
notes.27:36: Esau plays on the name Jacob (Ya'aqov) and the Qal verb 'aqav ("to grasp the heel, trip up, supplant"), echoing Jacob's naming at birth in Genesis 25:26.
notes.27:39: The Hebrew preposition min ("from") is deliberately ambiguous here, allowing either the privative sense "apart from" or "away from" (contrasting with Jacob's blessing in v. 28) or the partitive sense "of" or "from" (echoing v. 28).
notes.27:40: The rare Hiphil verb tarid (from rud) means "grow restless" or "roam restlessly," and the Qal verb paraqta literally means "tear off" or "wrench off."
notes.28:11: Hebrew literally reads "the place" with the definite article, signaling a specific location in the narrator's mind. The noun rendered "at his head" denotes the area around the head or a headrest rather than necessarily a pillow beneath it.
notes.28:12: The noun sullam ("stairway") occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible; derived from a root meaning "to heap up," it denotes a stepped ramp, stairway, or ladder.
notes.28:13: The prepositional phrase 'alav ("above it") can refer either to the stairway ("above it") or to Jacob ("beside him").
notes.28:21: Following standard Hebrew conditional syntax, the weqatal clause "then the LORD will be my God" begins the apodosis (result) of Jacob's vow; alternatively, it may close the condition ("and the LORD is my God"), with the vow's commitment beginning at v. 22.
notes.29:12: Hebrew literally reads "her father's brother," using the word for brother in the wider sense of a close male relative (as also in 29:15), since Jacob was Rebekah's son and thus Laban's nephew.
notes.29:17: The Hebrew adjective rendered "delicate" literally means soft or tender; applied to eyes only here in the Hebrew Bible, it is variously understood as describing weak, dull eyes or soft, gentle eyes.
notes.29:27: The Hebrew verb form can be parsed either as Qal first-person plural cohortative ("and we will give"), matching the direct object marker and Laban's "our place" in 29:26, or as Niphal third-person feminine singular ("and this one also will be given").
notes.29:31: The Qal passive participle "hated" (also in 29:33) is used in Hebrew idiomatic contrast with "loved" (29:30) to denote being unloved or less favored.
notes.29:34: Unlike 29:35 (third-person feminine singular, "she called"), the Masoretic text here has third-person masculine singular, functioning either as an indefinite subject ("his name was called") or referring to Jacob ("he called").
notes.30:8: The Hebrew phrase 'wrestlings of God' (naftule Elohim) pairs a cognate noun with the Niphal verb of patal ('wrestle') to play on the name Naphtali; 'of God' also functions as a Hebrew superlative idiom for mighty or fateful struggles.
notes.30:11: The translation follows the Qere (read text) ba gad ('Fortune has come') rather than the Ketiv (written text) begad ('In fortune' or 'How fortunate').
notes.30:20: Both the verb zabad ('bestow a gift') with its cognate noun zebed ('gift') and the verb zabal ('honor' or 'exalt,' traditionally 'dwell with') occur only here in the Hebrew Bible, forming a double wordplay on the name Zebulun.
notes.30:27: Laban's conditional clause breaks off without stating his request ('please stay'), a Hebrew rhetorical ellipsis; the Piel verb nichesh specifically denotes learning through divination or omens.
notes.30:41: In verses 41-42, 'sturdy' renders passive participles of qashar (literally 'bound tight,' Pual in v. 41 and Qal passive in v. 42), contrasted with 'feeble' from ataf (Hiphil infinitive and Qal passive participle in v. 42).
notes.31:13: Hebrew ha-el Bet-el is an unusual construct construction in which the first noun retains the definite article before a proper name, conveying "the God of Bethel."
notes.31:20: Literally "stole the heart (mind) of Laban," a Hebrew idiom for deceiving someone without their knowledge, playing on the verb "steal" (ganav) used in v. 19 and repeated in vv. 26, 27, 30, 32, and 39.
notes.31:39: The Piel verb achattennah (from chata, normally "sin") carries the restitutive sense "bear the loss of it." The two forms genuvti ("stolen") preserve the archaic construct ending -i (hireq compaginis) before "day" and "night."
notes.31:47: Laban gives the stone heap an Aramaic name (Jegar-sahadutha) and Jacob gives it the equivalent Hebrew name (Galeed); both mean "heap of witness."
notes.32:3: The Hebrew name Mahanaim is a dual form meaning "two camps," recalling the camp of God's angels and anticipating Jacob's division of his company into two camps in verse 8.
notes.32:11: Literally, "I am too small for all the acts of loyal love," using the Qal stative perfect of the root meaning "to be small" with a comparative preposition as an idiom for humility and unworthiness.
notes.32:21: The Hebrew repeats the noun panim, "face," four times in this verse: "appease his face," "ahead of me" (lit. "to my face"), "see his face," and "accept me" (lit. "lift up my face," an idiom for showing favor).
notes.32:32: The Masoretic Text spells the place name Peniel ("face of God") in verse 31 and Penuel in verse 32, using an archaic variant connecting vowel in the construct form.
notes.32:33: The rare Hebrew expression gid hannasheh occurs only in this verse and designates the sciatic nerve or hip sinew located along the socket of the hip joint.
notes.33:4: In the Masoretic Text, the verb "and kissed him" (wayyishshaqehu) bears six scribal dots (puncta extraordinaria) above its letters, a traditional mark indicating a textual or interpretive question concerning the word.
notes.33:14: Literally, "at the foot of the livestock ... and at the foot of the children"; the Hebrew idiom leregel signifies matching the walking pace of another, and melakah ("work" or "property") here denotes movable livestock.
notes.33:18: The Hebrew word shalem is translated here as an adverbial adjective meaning "safely" or "intact," echoing Jacob's vow in Genesis 28:21, though some ancient versions treat it as a place name, "Shalem."
notes.33:19: The Hebrew word qesitah (kesitah), appearing only three times in the Hebrew Bible (Gen 33:19; Josh 24:32; Job 42:11), refers to an ancient unit of weighed payment or monetary value of uncertain worth.
notes.33:20: The altar name El-Elohe-Israel means "God, the God of Israel" or "El is the God of Israel."
notes.34:2: The verb rendered 'violated her' (wayye'anneha, Piel of anah II) literally means 'humbled/humiliated her' and is used in Hebrew for sexual violation. The preceding form otah with shakhav ('lay') functions here like 'with her' (cf. 34:7).
notes.34:3: The phrase 'spoke to the heart of' (dibber al-lev) is a Hebrew idiom for speaking tenderly, persuasively, or reassuringly. Here and in 34:12 the word for 'young woman' exhibits the Pentateuchal spelling ha-na'ar pointed to be read ha-na'arah.
notes.34:21: The expression 'broad on every side' translates the Hebrew idiom rachavat-yadayim, literally 'wide of two hands,' signifying ample room in every direction.
notes.34:25: The adverbial noun betach ('in security') is syntactically ambiguous: it can describe the city as resting unsuspecting and off guard (as translated here), or it can describe Simeon and Levi as attacking boldly and without opposition.
notes.35:7: The verb 'revealed Himself' (niglu, Niphal perfect of galah) is grammatically plural in agreement with the plural form ha-Elohim ('God'), a rare Hebrew construction used for the one true God (cf. Gen 20:13).
notes.35:8: 'Allon-bacuth' means 'Oak of Weeping.' Here the tree is an oak (allon), distinct from the terebinth (elah) mentioned in 35:4.
notes.35:16: The phrase rendered 'some distance' (kivrat ha-aretz, literally 'a stretch of land') refers to an uncertain ancient measure of distance.
notes.35:18: 'Ben-oni' means 'Son of my sorrow' (or 'Son of my misfortune'), whereas 'Benjamin' (Binyamin) means 'Son of the right hand.'
notes.35:22: The Masoretic text carries double cantillation and a traditional mid-verse pause immediately after 'and Israel heard of it,' breaking off abruptly before introducing the list of Jacob's twelve sons.
notes.36:2: Hebrew bat ('daughter') here designates Oholibamah as the granddaughter of Zibeon (cf. vv. 24-25; similarly in v. 14), and the Masoretic text calls Zibeon 'the Hivite' rather than 'the Horite' (cf. vv. 20-21).
notes.36:5: The Qere (read form) is Jeush, matching v. 18, while the Ketiv (written consonants) reads Jeish; the same Ketiv/Qere variant occurs in v. 14.
notes.36:15: Hebrew alluf, related to elef ('thousand' or 'clan'), denotes the leader of a tribal clan; in v. 30 the plural phrase le-allufeihem literally means 'according to their chiefs' (that is, chief by chief or according to their chiefdoms).
notes.36:24: Hebrew ha-yemim occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible; its meaning is uncertain, though 'hot springs' is the prevailing scholarly understanding (ancient versions also suggest 'water' or 'mules').
notes.36:26: The Masoretic Hebrew reads Dishan here (identical to v. 28), whereas 1 Chronicles 1:41 and the Samaritan Pentateuch read Dishon, matching the fifth son of Seir in v. 21.
notes.37:3: Hebrew ketonet passim ("long-sleeved tunic") literally denotes a tunic of extremities, reaching the wrists and ankles (cf. 2 Sam 13:18-19), though ancient versions rendered it as an ornamented or multicolored garment.
notes.37:12: The Masoretic Text marks the direct-object particle et before "their father's flock" with extraordinary dots (puncta extraordinaria), an ancient scribal sign indicating traditional textual doubt or pause without altering the reading.
notes.37:28: The subject of the plural verbs "pulled," "brought up," and "sold" is grammatically unspecified in Hebrew and may refer either to the Midianite traders or to Joseph's brothers (cf. 37:36; 45:4).
notes.37:36: The Masoretic Text reads "Medanites" (from Medan, brother of Midian in Gen 25:2), whereas verse 28 has "Midianites"; scholars take this either as a kindred tribe or as a variant spelling of Midianites.
notes.38:8: "Fulfill the duty of a brother-in-law" translates the Piel denominative imperative yabbem (from yabam, brother-in-law), referring to the levirate marriage custom of raising an heir for a deceased childless brother (cf. Deut 25:5-10).
notes.38:9: Literally "he would ruin/waste toward the ground" (Piel weqatal shichet with directional artsah), leaving the object ("his seed") elliptical.
notes.38:21: Hirah uses qedeshah ("shrine prostitute," literally a consecrated woman) rather than zonah ("prostitute," v. 15); the place name Enaim (also v. 14) literally means "two springs."
notes.38:25: Tamar's imperative "Please identify" (hakker-na, Hiphil of nkr) and Judah's response "recognized" (wayyakker, v. 26) deliberately echo the exact Hebrew wording used in 37:32-33 regarding Joseph's tunic.
notes.38:29: The midwife's exclamation plays on the root prts ("break through" / "breach") to explain the name Perez, and alekha ("for yourself") can also mean "upon you." The verb wayyiqra ("his name was called," also v. 30) is an impersonal third-person masculine singular.
notes.39:9: The negative particle with a third-person masculine singular suffix (einennu, lit. "he is not") refers directly to Joseph's master, though some render it impersonally as "there is no one."
notes.39:11: Hebrew kehayyom hazzeh (lit. "like this day") is an idiom denoting an unspecified day in the narrative ("on a certain day").
notes.39:14: The Piel infinitive construct of tsachaq with the preposition be- literally means "to laugh or play at" and carries the sense of mocking, insulting, or taking improper liberties (compare Gen 26:8; 39:17).
notes.39:20: Ketiv/Qere variant: the written ketiv (asurei, Qal passive participle construct plural of asar) means "the bound ones of," while the read qere (asirei, noun construct plural of asir, translated here) means "the prisoners of"; both convey the same sense.
notes.40:13: The idiom "lift up the head" here signifies restoring the cupbearer to favor and rank, setting up a grim wordplay in v. 19 where adding "from off you" (me'alekha) turns the phrase into decapitation, and in v. 20 where it encompasses both officials' reckoning.
notes.40:15: The rare Pual infinitive absolute paired with the Pual finite verb (gunnov gunnavti) intensifies the passive statement ("truly stolen"). "The pit" (habbor) designates a subterranean dungeon and verbally echoes the pit into which Joseph's brothers threw him in Gen 37:24.
notes.40:16: The rare word chori is most often linked to a root meaning "white," denoting white bread or fine white cakes, though another view connects it to "hole" and renders "openwork" or "wicker baskets."
notes.40:20: Hebrew yom hulledet et-par'oh (lit. "the day of the being-born of Pharaoh") uses the Hophal infinitive construct of yalad with the marker et introducing the grammatical subject of the passive verb, a recognized Classical Hebrew construction.
notes.41:16: Hebrew bil'aday ("apart from me") disclaims human credit, followed by a wordplay on the Qal verb 'anah ("answered" ... "will answer") with shalom ("welfare/peace"), expressing that God Himself will provide an answer bringing peace to Pharaoh.
notes.41:34: The Piel denominative verb chimmesh (from chamesh, "five") means to take or levy a fifth part of the land's yield during the seven years of abundance.
notes.41:40: Hebrew 'al-pikha yishshaq is literally "by your mouth [all my people] shall kiss" (Qal imperfect of nashaq), an idiom for paying homage, ordering oneself, or submitting to authority.
notes.41:43: Hebrew 'abrek is likely an Egyptian loanword used as a public acclamation (perhaps "Pay attention!" or "Bow the knee!"), traditionally linked in Hebrew to the root barak ("kneel"). The clause "Thus he placed him" translates a Qal infinitive absolute (wenaton) continuing the preceding narrative verbs.
notes.41:56: The Masoretic Text reads literally "opened all that was in them," an elliptical expression for the grain depots holding Egypt's reserves. The Qal verb shabar here means "sold grain," whereas the same Qal root in 41:57 means "to buy grain."
notes.42:7: Wordplay on the Hebrew root nkr: the Hiphil verb ('recognized them') contrasts directly with the Hithpael ('acted as a stranger toward them').
notes.42:9: 'The nakedness of the land' is a literal Hebrew idiom referring to the land's exposed or undefended weak points.
notes.42:28: Literally 'their heart went out,' an idiom for losing courage in terror; the following clause ('trembling they turned to one another') uses a pregnant Hebrew construction combining the verb 'tremble' with the preposition 'to.'
notes.42:33: The Masoretic Text omits the noun 'grain' here, reading literally 'and the famine of your households take and go,' an elliptical phrasing for 'grain for the famine of your households' as in verse 19.
notes.43:11: 'Prized produce' translates a rare Hebrew noun (zimrah, found only here in this sense) denoting the choice or celebrated yield of the land; 'gum and myrrh' refer to aromatic botanical resins (likely tragacanth gum and labdanum).
notes.43:18: 'Rush upon us' translates the rare Hithpoel infinitive of the root meaning 'roll' (literally 'roll oneself upon'), idiomatically expressing an overwhelming assault or pretext for accusation.
notes.43:28: Ketiv/Qere: the written text (ketiv) lacks the second final waw and appears as a singular verb, while the read tradition (qere) reads the plural 'prostrated themselves,' agreeing with the preceding plural verb.
notes.43:34: 'Five times greater' is literally 'five hands'; 'drank freely' translates the Qal of skr, which ranges from drinking to full satisfaction to becoming intoxicated.
notes.44:5: The Masoretic Hebrew begins directly with "Is this not the one...", whereas the Septuagint adds "Why have you stolen my silver cup?" before it. The phrase "indeed practices divination" renders the Piel infinitive absolute plus Piel imperfect of the verb for practicing divination, repeated in 44:15.
notes.44:16: The verb "justify ourselves" is the Hithpael imperfect of the root for righteousness, showing consonant metathesis and emphatic assimilation with the prefix. Judah also plays on the Hebrew noun for servant and slave, using the same word both for courtly self-reference ("your servants") and for actual bondage ("slaves to my lord"), as again in 44:33.
notes.44:28: The emphatic phrase "has been torn to pieces" pairs a Qal infinitive absolute with a Pual perfect passive of the verb for tearing prey, intensifying the certainty of the passive action.
notes.44:34: The closing clause uses the conjunction of apprehension independently to express urgent dread ("Let me not look upon..."), and "find" echoes the key verb for finding repeated throughout the chapter.
notes.45:1: The infinitive construct "when Joseph made himself known" is a Hithpael form of the verb meaning "to know" that preserves its historical initial waw as a consonant.
notes.45:5: The phrase "do not be angry with yourselves" renders an idiom literally meaning "do not let it burn in your eyes", and "for the preservation of life" translates a noun cognate with the verb "to keep alive" in 45:7.
notes.45:7: The closing phrase "to keep you alive for a great deliverance" uses a Hiphil infinitive construct of the verb "to live" followed by a prepositional phrase that can denote either the result ("for a great deliverance") or the resulting group ("as a great company of survivors").
notes.45:19: The Masoretic Hebrew reads a second-person singular Pual passive ("Now as for you, you are commanded"), whereby Pharaoh authorizes Joseph to issue the directive, whereas the Septuagint renders an active imperative ("Now command them").
notes.45:24: The command "Do not become agitated" uses a Qal verb denoting trembling, agitation, or angry excitement, which in this context encompasses both anxious distress and quarreling among the brothers.
notes.46:3: Hebrew meredah is an unusual Qal infinitive construct of yarad ("go down") with a feminine ending, following the preposition min ("from"), literally "from going down."
notes.46:4: Hebrew combines a Hiphil imperfect of alah ("bring up") with the emphatic particle gam and a Qal infinitive absolute of the same root (aloh) to express emphatic certainty ("also surely bring you up"). "Place his hand on your eyes" is a literal idiom for closing the eyes of a dying parent.
notes.46:20: The singular Niphal passive verb ("was born") takes the object marker et before the compound subject ("Manasseh and Ephraim"), a standard Classical Hebrew impersonal passive construction.
notes.46:28: Masoretic Hebrew reads lehorot, the Hiphil infinitive construct of yarah ("to direct" or "show the way"), whereas the Septuagint reflects a different verbal root meaning "to meet."
notes.47:13: Hebrew wattelah is the Qal wayyiqtol of the rare verb lahah ("grow faint, languish"), occurring as a finite verb only here in the Hebrew Bible.
notes.47:17: Hebrew wayenahalem is the Piel wayyiqtol of nahal, which normally means "lead" or "guide gently," used here in the extended sense of providing for or carrying people through hardship.
notes.47:21: Masoretic Hebrew reads the Hiphil of abar ("relocated/moved") with "to the cities," whereas the Samaritan Pentateuch and Septuagint reflect a single-consonant difference yielding the Hiphil of abad ("reduced to servitude as slaves").
notes.47:23: Hebrew he ("here is") is a rare presentative interjection occurring only here and in Ezekiel 16:43 in the Hebrew Bible, cognate with Biblical Aramaic ha.
notes.47:31: Masoretic vocalization reads ham-mittah ("the bed"), whereas the Septuagint (followed in Hebrews 11:21) vocalizes the same unpointed consonants as ham-matteh ("the staff").
notes.48:7: Hebrew metah alai (lit. "died upon me") is an idiom expressing bereavement and painful personal loss.
notes.48:14: The rare Piel verb sikkel occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and is generally understood as "crossing" (from a Semitic cognate meaning "intertwine"), though some connect it with the root for insight ("guiding knowingly").
notes.48:16: The Piel jussive verb yevarekh ("may He bless") is singular despite following both "the God" (v. 15) and "the Angel," uniting them in the blessing; the unique Qal verb yidgu ("may they teem") is related to the noun for fish, conveying prolific growth.
notes.48:22: Hebrew shekhem ("ridge, shoulder, portion") forms a deliberate wordplay with the place name Shechem, where Joseph was later buried (Josh 24:32).
notes.49:4: The hapax noun pachaz denotes reckless turbulence or boiling over; the verse abruptly shifts from second person ("you defiled") to third person (alah, "he went up") as Jacob turns in indignation.
notes.49:5: The rare noun mekherotehem occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible; it is most often understood as "blades" or "swords," though some scholars interpret it as "schemes" or "agreements."
notes.49:10: The Masoretic text reads the single word Shiloh, traditionally taken as a messianic title or place name; several ancient versions understand it as shelloh, "the one to whom it belongs" (cf. Ezek 21:27).
notes.49:21: Following the Masoretic vocalization ("doe" and "words of beauty"); with altered vocalization of the same consonants, some interpreters read either "that bears lovely fawns" or "a spreading terebinth that yields lovely branches."
notes.49:26: The Masoretic text vocalizes horai ("my progenitors") followed by ad-ta'avat ("as far as the limit/bounty of"); by redividing and repointing horai ad, the Septuagint and several modern versions read "the ancient mountains."
notes.50:11: The name Abel-mizraim (meaning "meadow of Egypt" or "watercourse of Egypt") creates a wordplay with the similar-sounding Hebrew word for "mourning" used earlier in the verse. The verb rendered "its name was called" is literally an impersonal active singular, "one called its name."
notes.50:13: The clause rendered "the field that Abraham had purchased" treats the Hebrew phrase "the field" as a clarifying direct object; alternatively, reading the particle et as the preposition "with," it may be translated "which Abraham had purchased together with the field."
notes.50:16: The verb translated "sent word" is literally "ordered" or "charged" (Piel of tsavah) followed by "to Joseph," an idiomatic ellipsis for instructing messengers to deliver a message.
notes.50:21: Literally "spoke upon their heart" (with singular collective "heart"), a Hebrew idiom denoting tender, reassuring speech.
notes.50:26: The verb rendered "he was placed" is an unusual passive wayyiqtol form, generally analyzed as an archaic Qal passive related to the root sim ("to place/put"). In Hebrew, "coffin" carries the definite article to indicate the customary burial chest.

unplaced.text: And Laban said to Jacob, "Look at this heap, and look at the pillar that I have set up between me and you.
unplaced.note: The first-person verb yariti ("I have set up") is translated as written: Laban claims credit for establishing the boundary marker, although Jacob set up the pillar (31:45).
